meta.title: Conflict Watchlist
meta.notes: Fully automated register: a scheduled open-source review rewrites this file daily (procedure in docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md) and an hourly GitHub Action refreshes the live reporting feed (watchlist-live.json) from GDELT. Every comparison the dashboard shows (state moves, changed dimensions, the attention-score bonuses) is made against the register as it stood compareDays (7) days ago, taken from each item's `snapshots` (one entry per review: date, state and the five dimensions). Each review: (1) set reviewDate/previousReviewDate, (2) for every item set the new `now` on the five dimensions and the new `state`, then append today's snapshot (keep the last 60), (3) rewrite `status` (`summary`: plain-language current status whose first sentence states the newest development; `sources`: 2–3 links to the newest reporting), `whyNow`, `topic` and `whyMatters` (stable framing, revise only on a phase change), `changes` (dated bullets covering the last 7 days: keep those still inside the window, add today's, drop older ones), `next`, `ignore` and `sources`, (4) record any state move in `history` and keep `timeline` (4–8 dated one-line events of the current phase, chronological) current. The dashboard derives attention rank, movements, changed-dimension flags, staleness, coverage surges — do not type those in. `next` holds named, checkable indicators.

phase.label: Conflict phase
phase.desc: A short label for the stage the conflict is in (for example attritional war, ceasefire without implementation, grey-zone contest). It sits under the current-status summary and shows the label from 7 days ago when it changed.

escalation.label: Escalation risk
escalation.desc: How likely a step up in intensity or a change of phase is in the coming weeks.

levels.Low: Stable; no live trigger and restraints hold.
levels.Moderate: Triggers exist (deadlines, disputes, incidents) but restraints are holding.
levels.High: Active exchanges or a named trigger that is likely to fire; a phase change is plausible within weeks.
levels.Severe: Active war or ongoing kinetic exchange with strategic stakes (major shipping lanes, energy, great-power forces).

tempo.label: Operational tempo
tempo.desc: How much military activity is actually happening in the review window.

levels.Medium: Recurring incidents or steady, limited operations (patrols, fortification, occasional strikes).
levels.High: Daily strikes or operations across fronts.

adaptation.label: Adaptation behaviour
adaptation.desc: How much new tactical or technical behaviour appeared in the window; this is where the Army learning sits.

levels.Low: Both sides are using the same methods as before.
levels.High: Novel, repeatable adaptations appeared (new weapons employment, counter-measures, doctrine shifts).

sgExposure.label: Singapore exposure
sgExposure.desc: How directly the conflict touches Singapore's interests. Not shown as a register column; it still feeds the attention score and the expanded row.

levels.Moderate: An ASEAN or diplomatic role, observer contributions, or supply-chain spillover.
levels.High: Direct effect on sea lanes, energy or shipping, a Singapore-flagged vessel affected, or relevance to deployments.

attentionScore.desc: Deterministic, explainable rank. state (Priority 40 / Active 25 / Watch 10 / Archive 0) + escalation risk (Severe 20 / High 15 / Moderate 8 / Low 2) + 5 per dimension that changed over the last 7 days (compareDays) + 10 if the state moved up over the same window + Singapore exposure (High 8 / Moderate 4 / Low 0) + tier (T1 6 / T2 3 / T3 0) + 8 if the live open-source feed shows a coverage surge (see definitions.feed.surgeRule). Items flagged ignore-for-now are shown but ranked last.

feed.source: GDELT DOC 2.0 API (open, no key). Per item: 30-day daily article counts (TimelineVolRaw) and the most relevant English-language articles of the last 7 days (ArtList, HybridRel). Synced by .github/workflows/sync-watchlist-feed.yml into watchlist-live.json.
feed.surgeRule: A coverage surge is flagged when the last 7 days carry at least twice the article volume of the 7 days before and at least 20 articles; a surge adds 8 points to the attention score.
feed.titleFilter: Articles are kept only when the title contains one of the item's terms, to cut GDELT's full-text noise.
feed.terms: Title filter: at least one of these substrings must appear in an article title for it to count as reporting on the item.
feed.require: Optional groups of substrings; a title must contain at least one term from every group (two-party theatres: one term per side).
feed.exclude: Optional substrings that drop a title (sport, entertainment and other noise), in addition to the sync's global list.
feed.spamDomainsNote: Article sources dropped outright (livestream/score spam). The daily review adds domains seen producing noise.

columns.tier: Standing relevance to the Army: T1 Priority Conflicts, T2 Active Regional & Escalation Watches, T3 Baseline Regional Research Reserve. Tiers do not change week to week.
columns.state: Today's monitoring state: Priority (direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value), Active (material trend, escalation or regional relevance), Watch (baseline monitoring), Archive (reserve; revisit on a named trigger). ▲▼ marks a move over the last 7 days.
columns.status: Current status: the newest title-matched headline from the live open-source feed (synced hourly) on top, then a plain-language summary of what is happening now whose first sentence states the newest development, with links to the newest reporting it rests on. The phase label sits beneath; a struck-through label is the phase 7 days ago.
columns.coverage: Open-source coverage from the live feed (GDELT with Google News fallback): the sparkline is the last 30 days (or four weekly counts), the number is articles in the last 7 days with the change against the 7 before. 'Surge' = at least twice the prior week and at least 20 articles. Refreshes hourly.
columns.nextIndicator: The soonest dated indicator to watch, tagged with the numbered topic and watch area it informs (or 'cross-cutting' when it bears on the theatre as a whole). Expand the row for the full list.
columns.confidence: How well-sourced the assessment is: High (multiple independent, dated sources), Medium (some single-source or snippet-only items), Low (thin or contested reporting).
columns.attention: Attention score, the register's sort order. Hover a score for its breakdown.
columns.topic: Topics of interest: the three capability contests the Army follows this theatre for, set by the team (from the watchlist workbook). Numbered so they line up with the 'Why it matters' and 'Watch areas' columns; the chip is the topic's adaptability rating.
columns.whyMatters: Why it matters here: for each numbered topic, what the theatre tests (the capability, behaviour or mechanism under study).
columns.watchAreas: Watch areas: for each numbered topic, its watch status and what to monitor. Status tags: Rising (activity increasing), Established (steady pattern), Contested (the outcome is still open), Watch for trigger (review only on a named event), Background monitor, Declining.
columns.adaptability: Adaptability: how transferable the topic's lessons are to the Army — High, Medium or Low, set by the team.

infoOps.desc: Information operations and strategic communications watch. Switched on for an item when a trigger event (a summit, a crisis) makes messaging and influence activity worth tracking on its own: a narrower hourly feed of reporting on official messaging, state-media narratives and documented influence campaigns, plus dated findings and an assessment researched daily from open sources.

types.official statement: Government, foreign-ministry, military or party statement aimed at an audience (strategic communications).
types.state-media narrative: Framing pushed by state or party media, including English-language outlets aimed abroad.
types.covert information operation: Documented coordinated inauthentic behaviour, disinformation or cognitive-warfare activity, attributed by a credible reporter.
types.coercive signalling: Military, coast-guard or legal action whose purpose is the message it sends.
types.sanctions/lawfare: Sanctions, lists or legal framing used to pressure or delegitimise.
types.counter-messaging: The targeted side's official response or rebuttal.
types.domestic narrative: Narratives inside the targeted polity (parties, polls, viral claims).
types.debunked claim: A specific false claim identified by a fact-checker.
types.third-party assessment: Analysis by a think-tank, researcher or major outlet.

items.whyNow: On 28 Sep Russia struck Kyiv in daylight with jet drones, hitting the National Academy of Sciences, a medical facility and a pharmaceutical company, killing one in the capital and four in Dnipro with 124 drones flown between 06:30 and 18:30, 86 of them jet-powered, while Zelensky said Russia has already begun 'additional mobilisation', Putin decreed a 15,500-strong increase in the armed forces and HUR counted over 8,000 North Korean troops in Russia with 10,000 more being selected; Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps closed Vivaldi's third stage with 51 sq km, three settlements and over 250 prisoners taken using converted BTR-60s as kamikaze ground drones, and ISW read a Kremlin-linked milblogger's endorsement of a strike-led theory of victory as confirmation that Russia's winter campaign is meant to be decisive by spring 2027.
changes: 28 Sep: A Russian jet drone hit the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv in a daytime raid, killing an assistant to 87-year-old former security council secretary Volodymyr Horbulin, who was slightly wounded, with 19 injured in the capital (Klitschko) and a pharmaceutical company, petrol stations and a medical facility also hit; four were killed and at least 19 wounded at a Dnipro business centre, 30 civilians were wounded in Zaporizhzhia, a Kharkiv guided bomb injured at least 22 including six children, and an ice-cream factory in Zhytomyr region and a checkpoint at Starovoitove near the Polish border were struck; the Air Force said Russia flew 124 drones between 06:30 and 18:30, 86 of them jet-powered, of which 86 (49 jet-powered) were downed with hits at 27 locations, after 112 of 165 overnight drones were downed (single source); Al Jazeera counted eight killed nationwide over 27–28 Sep, RTE/Reuters five on 28 Sep alone, so the counts differ (Reuters via RTE, Al Jazeera, Ukrinform, Ukrainska Pravda).

28 Sep: Zelensky said 'the Russians have already begun additional mobilisation', increasing recruitment 'by different methods' and seeking more foreigners, as Putin signed a decree raising the armed forces by 15,500 to 2,441,630 personnel (1,550,500 military), the fourth increase this year; HUR said over 8,000 North Korean troops are in Russia, 10,000 more are being selected for training and deployment with a long-term contingent of up to 50,000, and that Russia is helping Pyongyang set up Shahed-type drone production; Zelensky put overall drone interception at 70% but jet drones at 57%, and said the Shahed wave shows Russia is not preparing to de-escalate (Kyiv Independent, Ukrinform, Kyiv Post, Al Jazeera).

28 Sep: The 3rd Army Corps said Vivaldi's third stage recovered 51 sq km (176 sq km since 15 Sep), liberated Ridkodub, Nove and Katerynivka, restored full control of Karpivka and Novomykhailivka, inflicted over 2,000 Russian casualties and took over 250 prisoners including officers, pilots and artillerymen, using Soviet BTR-60s converted into unmanned kamikaze vehicles to breach fortifications and a deception that made Russian reserves counter-attack on the Shandryholove–Zelena Dolyna axis while the main blow took the high ground at Nove; Biletsky called the stage 'a turning point for the entire operation' and said entire Russian units surrendered in full (Kyiv Independent, Kyiv Post, Ukrainska Pravda).

27 Sep: ISW assessed that a prominent Kremlin-affiliated milblogger has embraced Putin's theory of victory through expansive combined ballistic-missile and jet-drone strikes to force capitulation by spring 2027, while conceding the front is 'static'; that the Kremlin may postpone large-scale involuntary mobilisation until the strike campaign's results are in, though casualty replacement may force it sooner; that Russian forces are conducting fighting withdrawals across the Zherebets river near Lyman, Ukrainian marines cleared about 5 sq km south of Dobropillia and Ukrainian forces advanced in southwestern Chasiv Yar; that a likely Russian object crossed Romanian airspace near the Danube Delta on 26–27 Sep; and that German investigators suspect the GRU in incendiary attacks on Munich defence firms; Ukraine intercepted about 55% of 2,730 Shaheds in September, and Ukrainian drones hit the Pavlovskaya oil depot in Krasnodar (ISW/Critical Threats, Al Jazeera).

27 Sep: Russian drones and missiles hit Kyiv for a fourth consecutive night, killing two at the Stolichny market, striking a data centre twice and Kyivstar's headquarters, with Russia's defence ministry confirming a strike on a Vodafone Ukraine data centre and outages for about 100,000 households; Zelensky counted 277 drones in 24 hours, 155 jet-powered, and 10,660 Russian casualties in the week; Lavrov told UNGA Moscow will continue 'to the end' and dismissed the first Russian–German foreign-minister meeting since 2022 (Kyiv Independent, Reuters via Moscow Times, AP via ABC News, Kyiv Post).

26 Sep: Russia launched 173 drones, about 50 jet-powered, killing four; Ukraine's General Staff reported hits on the Azov optical-mechanical plant and the Ilsky refinery; Zelensky said Russia will spend $12bn on jet drones and loitering munitions in 2027 (single source) and Trump declined to confirm the Patriot production licence he had announced on 25 Sep; ISW assessed Ukraine's 2026 gains may be forcing Putin onto a winter long-range-strike theory of victory (Al Jazeera, Kyiv Independent, CNN, ISW via Kyiv Post).

timeline.text: Russia hit Kyiv with 32 cruise missiles and 166 Shahed-type drones, over half jet-powered, killing five and ending the three-day pause declared during US envoys Witkoff and Kushner's visits to Moscow and Kyiv.
Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps revealed Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive near Lyman it said cleared 75 square kilometres of Russian infiltrators and liberated Serednie and nearby villages.

A Ukrainian drone strike set both crude distillation units ablaze at Gazprom Neft's Moscow refinery, followed on 22 September by strikes on the Ufa and Samara refineries more than 900 kilometres from the border.

Zelensky met Trump at the UN General Assembly and offered a reciprocal energy ceasefire, which Lavrov answered the next day by saying Russia would not pause its operation during negotiations in any format.
Russia launched 282 drones and three waves of ballistic and Zircon missiles, killing 16 people across Ukraine including two in Kyiv, while suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova.

Russian drones killed seven people in Kyiv as Ukraine's General Staff confirmed strikes on the Lukoil Perm refinery 1,450 kilometres from the border, and Kyiv and the Kremlin both confirmed a US proposal for technical-level trilateral talks.

On the fourth consecutive night of strikes on Kyiv Russia launched 277 drones in 24 hours, 155 of them jet-powered, hit a Kyiv data centre twice and Kyivstar's headquarters, and Lavrov dismissed German de-escalation calls, while Zelensky said Operation Vivaldi had recovered 125 square kilometres north of Lyman.

A daylight Russian jet-drone raid hit Kyiv's National Academy of Sciences and killed five people across Ukraine, Zelensky said Russia had begun additional mobilisation as Putin enlarged the armed forces by 15,500, and the 3rd Army Corps closed Vivaldi's third stage with 51 square kilometres, three settlements and over 250 prisoners taken using converted BTR-60s as kamikaze vehicles.

text: On persistent ISR versus signature management and deception, the Established and Contested status is borne out from the Ukrainian side: the 3rd Army Corps said on 28 Sep that Vivaldi’s third stage recovered 51 sq km and over 250 prisoners because Russian reserves were drawn onto a feint at Shandryholove–Zelena Dolyna while the main blow took Nove, and ISW on 27 Sep recorded Russian fighting withdrawals across the Zherebets. Deception is producing repeatable local uncertainty against an observer blinded by its own false reporting. On EW versus alternative UAS control and layered counter-UAS, the Rising rating holds and the contest is numerical: 86 of 124 daytime drones on 28 Sep were jet-powered, Zelensky put interception at 57% for jet types against 70% overall, and ISW on 27 Sep judged that Putin’s spring-2027 theory of victory depends on that penetration rate outrunning Ukraine’s interceptor-drone programme, due for mass deployment within months (single source).

On contested sustainment versus dispersed support and repair, the Established and Contested status hardens. Russia’s campaign moved from data centres and Kyivstar on 23–27 Sep to a daylight raid on the Academy of Sciences, a medical facility and a pharmaceutical firm on 28 Sep, while Ukraine’s expendable BTR-60 breaching vehicles show dispersed workshops turning legacy stock into unmanned effects; Moscow answers with force generation: a 15,500 decree and 10,000 more North Korean troops on 28 Sep.

items.whyNow: On 28 Sep the IDF and Shin Bet put the Gaza and 99th divisions on heightened alert over specific intelligence that Hamas plans to seize a soldier from one of the 40 unfenced Yellow Line positions to 'create another Gilad Shalit' before the Israeli and US elections, security officials told Channel 12 that an expanded operation may be 'a foregone conclusion', strikes killed two women in Gaza City and Nuseirat and the IDF said it had killed Hamas sniper Adi Adil Abd al-Aaser on 27 Sep, while Netanyahu flew secretly to Abu Dhabi to ask Mohammed bin Zayed to deny the pre-7 Oct warning, the EU extended EUBAM Rafah and EUPOL COPPS to June 2027, WAFA put the toll at 74,018 with 1,417 killed since the truce and the New York Times published satellite analysis of continued Israeli expansion inside Gaza.
changes: 28 Sep: Israeli strikes killed at least two Palestinians, a woman hit on her building's rooftop in Gaza City, whose husband and others were wounded, and a woman in Nuseirat camp, where the IDF said it struck a militant; WAFA put the toll at 74,018 killed and 175,079 wounded, with 1,417 killed and 4,964 wounded since the 11 Oct 2025 truce and 834 bodies recovered, while Reuters cited 'at least 1,400' since the ceasefire and four Israeli soldiers killed; the IDF said a 27 Sep strike in southern Gaza killed Hamas military-wing sniper Adi Adil Abd al-Aaser, accused of 'advancing attacks and attempting to restore Hamas capabilities' (Reuters via Arab News, Haaretz, WAFA, Times of Israel, CGTN).

28 Sep: The IDF and Shin Bet raised readiness in the Gaza territorial division and the 99th Division after specific intelligence that Hamas intends to kidnap a soldier from a Yellow Line position, of which 40 sit inside the line and 10 outside the fence with no physical barrier; a senior officer said Hamas wants 'another Gilad Shalit' before the Israeli and US elections and believes Israel cannot respond until after the November US vote, commanders were ordered to stay in sector and run vigilance checks, and Southern Command said over 600 Hamas operatives have been killed in the past year; security officials told Channel 12 that Hamas is tightening its grip on the population and an expanded operation 'may be a foregone conclusion', a Southern Command source saying 'the operations will continue as long as necessary' (ynet, i24NEWS, Israel National News, Times of Israel).

28 Sep: Netanyahu flew by private plane to Abu Dhabi for about four hours and met Mohammed bin Zayed for an hour, with Mossad chief Gofman present, to ask him to deny the Haaretz report that he warned of a major Hamas operation about ten days before 7 Oct 2023, according to AP sources, Channel 12 and Haaretz; the UAE confirmed the meeting and said it covered 'bilateral relations', Netanyahu's office called the reports 'fake news' and also denied that Egypt's former intelligence chief Abbas Kamel had warned him days before the attack; the New York Times published satellite analysis under the headline that Israel keeps expanding into Gaza despite the ceasefire (details not verified, single source); the EU Council renewed EUBAM Rafah and EUPOL COPPS to 30 June 2027, noting Rafah has operated on a limited basis since February and restating readiness to support the Gaza peace plan; settlers attacked a Palestinian car near al-Mughayyir, injuring an infant (Times of Israel, Haaretz, CNN, Brussels Times).

27 Sep: The IDF and Shin Bet said a 26 Sep strike in Nuseirat killed Saher Nidal Saqr, filmed carrying Noa Argamani and Avinatan Or into Gaza on 7 Oct 2023, and that a 22 Sep strike in northern Gaza killed Hamas commander Muhammad Ghabain, who held nine hostages; strikes killed two Palestinians in Gaza City and al-Mawasi as Gaza's health ministry passed 74,016 dead; Smotrich called for Israel to 'go to war' in the West Bank and annex up to the Yellow Line, which Egypt rejected the same day; UNRWA acting chief Saunders said the agency's capabilities are 'difficult to replicate' after the Board of Peace's exclusion; the Jerusalem Post reported the Atalef drone that killed two reservists on 24 Sep had seven prior non-detonations; Israel Hayom reported that a former Haniyeh bodyguard granted UK citizenship was arrested in London under a German warrant over a plot against Jewish targets in Germany and Austria, unconnected to the RAF Fairford arrests (Times of Israel, ynet, AP via ABC News, Al Jazeera, Jerusalem Post, Israel Hayom).

26 Sep: The IDF said strikes in Nuseirat and Khan Younis killed Nukhba member Ibrahim Mohsen and Hamas operative Mohammed Mohsen, both accused of restoring Hamas infrastructure; an evening drone strike west of Nuseirat killed a Palestinian; Hamas's Hazem Qassem called the Board of Peace's refusal to work with UNRWA 'complete alignment with the Zionist position' and Khalil al-Hayya said the roadmap, weapons included, must be implemented 'as a package' (Times of Israel, Anadolu, WAFA, Al Jazeera).

25 Sep: An Israeli strike on a vehicle at the Wijdan displacement camp in al-Mawasi killed one Palestinian; the IDF grounded all small explosive drones for 48 hours after two reservists were killed on 24 Sep by their own Atalef FPV; the IDF and Shin Bet said they have killed 16 key Hamas financial officers; the New York Times corroborated Haaretz's report of the UAE warning before 7 Oct, which Netanyahu's office denies; the Board of Peace said UNRWA will have no role in Gaza (Arab News, Times of Israel, JNS, Haaretz).

timeline.text: The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, endorsing the US Gaza plan, welcoming the Board of Peace and authorising an International Stabilization Force for Gaza.
Israel's security cabinet approved entry of an initial International Stabilization Force of about 200 personnel from countries such as Uganda and Morocco, operating in coordination with the IDF.
Hamas approved the Board of Peace's plan pairing gradual disarmament with phased Israeli withdrawal, a plan Netanyahu rejected pending genuine disarmament.
UN humanitarian officials said Israel had pushed the yellow line inward, leaving Palestinians under 40 percent of Gaza, with 1,334 killed since the ceasefire.

The Board of Peace unveiled a $2.4bn, 66-project reconstruction plan conditioned on Hamas disarmament, while an Israeli strike in western Khan Younis killed senior Hamas finance official Mohammad Abu Elwan among seven dead that day.

Netanyahu told the UN General Assembly that genocide allegations are the biggest lie of the century, while Tony Blair told a Board of Peace event that Hamas had agreed to the destruction of its tunnels and weapons factories and Hamas demanded entry of the technocratic committee and the international force.

The IDF and Shin Bet confirmed that a Nuseirat strike had killed a man filmed abducting Noa Argamani on 7 October 2023 and that a Hamas commander who held nine hostages had died in northern Gaza, as two more Palestinians were killed, the toll passed 74,000 and Smotrich called for a Gaza-style war in the West Bank.

The IDF and Shin Bet put two divisions on alert over intelligence that Hamas plans to abduct a soldier from a Yellow Line position and officials said an expanded operation may be unavoidable, as strikes killed two women in Gaza City and Nuseirat, Netanyahu flew secretly to Abu Dhabi over the pre-7 October warning reports and the EU extended its Rafah and West Bank police missions to June 2027.

text: On dense urban operations versus dispersed and concealed networks, the Established and Contested status is borne out: Southern Command said on 28 Sep it has killed over 600 operatives in a year, including a sniper on 27 Sep, yet the same day the IDF and Shin Bet raised two divisions’ readiness over specific intelligence that Hamas plans to seize a soldier from one of 40 unfenced Yellow Line positions, and officials called an expanded operation possibly ‘a foregone conclusion’. The concealed network still generates offensive options; static unfenced outposts are the exposed signature. On persistent ISR and precision strike versus civilian protection and legitimacy, the Contested status holds: the two people killed on 28 Sep were women, one on her rooftop in Gaza City, WAFA’s count since the truce reached 1,417 against the health ministry’s 1,145 via AP on 27 Sep, and Netanyahu’s secret 28 Sep trip to Abu Dhabi to seek a denial of the pre-7 Oct warning shows the legitimacy fight has moved to the origins of the war.

timeline.text: The US and Iran signed a 14-point memorandum of understanding that lifted the US naval blockade, reopened the Strait of Hormuz and opened a 60-day negotiating period.
After Iranian strikes on vessels collapsed the June ceasefire, US Central Command resumed its naval blockade of Iranian ports and struck Iranian anti-shipping targets near Hormuz.

After US strikes on Iranian coastal radars killed 11 people and the IRGC fired anti-ship ballistic missiles at a US carrier and destroyer, CENTCOM destroyed or disabled three Iranian tankers, the Downy, Stark 1 and Kylo.

An Iranian anti-ship cruise missile struck a non-Navy vessel carrying a Marine battalion landing team in the Strait of Hormuz, injuring eight Marines, an attack the Pentagon did not announce until NBC News reported it two weeks later.

A day after Witkoff and Kushner held Qatari-mediated talks with Araghchi in New York, Iran handed the US a written road map for a regionwide ceasefire and phased Hormuz reopening, while the bulk carrier Cape Dao was hit off Musandam and one seafarer was killed.

Foreign Minister Araghchi put a 'concrete' seven-day plan to Washington to end hostilities, lift the blockade and reopen Hormuz before nuclear talks, a senior official ruled out any nuclear concessions, and Iraq's four airports cut all Iranian flights under US sanctions.

Trump publicly rejected Iran's seven-day plan after the Wall Street Journal reported he expects to resume bombing after the November midterms, and the next day the IRGC claimed a second US underwater drone captured in the strait, which CENTCOM called 'clearly desperate'.

Araghchi met Qatari mediators and the UN secretary-general in New York as Qatar carried an amended seven-day plan to the US side and Trump said messages had been exchanged, while Iran's army chief of staff claimed full naval control of the strait.

timeline.text: The United States, Israel and Lebanon signed a US-brokered Trilateral Framework tying phased Israeli withdrawal to Hezbollah disarmament and creating a trilateral military coordination group.
Lebanese army troops deployed in Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, the first of three US-supervised pilot zones, after Israeli forces pulled back from the village.
Israel detonated about 1,100 tonnes of explosives to destroy Hezbollah tunnels under Ali al-Taher ridge and declared its south Lebanon security zone complete.

Israeli tanks and stun grenades forced Lebanese soldiers off a new post outside Deir Mimas that Israel said lay inside its Yellow Line, and the dispute was referred to the Military Technical Committee.

Salam told the UN General Assembly that Israel must withdraw to the recognised borders and that weapons must be held by the state alone, a day after asking for a Security Council-mandated presence to avoid a vacuum after UNIFIL, while Israeli strikes, shelling and a mass detonation at Deir Seryan continued and the IDF fired an interceptor at what it later called a false identification.

The IDF struck a Hezbollah weapons store at Sejoud to remove what it called a threat to its troops in the security zone, artillery and reported phosphorus shelling continued across Tyre, Bint Jbeil and Nabatieh districts, and Western diplomats said Washington had blocked a six-month UNIFIL extension and wants the Lebanese army to hold the border alone.

Hezbollah launched an explosive drone at Israeli troops inside the security zone overnight without causing casualties, the Israeli air force struck drone and anti-tank launch sites across nine southern localities in response, and Qassem told a Nasrallah-anniversary crowd that resistance continues until full expulsion and that Israel must first liberate the south before any dialogue.

Salam asked Rubio in Washington for a timeline for full Israeli withdrawal, Lebanese army deployment into the pilot zones and a credible verification mechanism and was told the framework is the only path to a durable peace, while the Israeli army levelled much of Mansouri in a mass detonation it said destroyed 600 infrastructure sites and eight tunnels, fired on two men entering its security zone, and UN peacekeepers reported 143 Israeli air violations over three days with no Hezbollah fire detected.

text: On border-zone security versus rocket, drone and dispersed-launch threats, the Established and Contested reading holds but fire is one-sided: UNIFIL told the UN on 28 Sep that it recorded 143 Israeli air violations and 166 projectile trajectories between 25 and 27 Sep and detected no Hezbollah rocket or artillery launches, while the only Hezbollah action in the window was the 27 Sep explosive drone, without casualties. The threat inside the zone is drones and roadside bombs, not rockets, and the 28 Sep shooting of two men approaching Israeli troops shows how thin the identification margin is. On precision strike versus escalation control, the pattern is contradicted: the 27 Sep response was framed as removing launch sites, but the 28 Sep detonation that levelled Mansouri, which the army says destroyed 600 sites and eight tunnels, follows Khiam (23 and 26 Sep), Bint Jbeil and Deir Seryan (25 Sep) and makes village-scale demolition, not precision, the dominant method.

On ceasefire monitoring versus armed-group reconstitution, the trigger is close: Salam asked Rubio on 28 Sep for a withdrawal timeline and a credible verification mechanism and received only 'only path to durable peace' language, Israel is reported the same day to want a US-led force mandated to disarm Hezbollah (single source), and a Jerusalem Post report relayed on 28 Sep judges Hezbollah's command structure still unrebuilt (Israeli source); adaptability stays Medium.

timeline.text: Thailand and Cambodia signed a ceasefire taking effect at noon, ending 20 days of fighting that killed over 100 people and displaced more than half a million.
Thailand's armed forces chief announced completion of the first 1.3 km of a permanent concrete border wall in Chanthaburi's Pong Nam Ron district, with over 7 km more planned.
Cambodia and Thailand delivered opening statements in Singapore before a UNCLOS Annex V conciliation commission on their overlapping claims in the Gulf of Thailand.

The first Singapore conciliation session closed with Cambodia tabling three settlement options and Thailand insisting a maritime boundary be delimited before any resource sharing; a second meeting was set for The Hague in October.
Cambodia formally protested a Buddha statue that Thai troops and monks placed on 18 September at Phnom Beng in Anlong Veng, calling it a fait accompli on occupied land.

Hun Manet told an international anti-scam conference in Phnom Penh that scam crackdowns must not become a pretext for military force against a neighbour; Thailand replied the next day by demanding implementation of the anti-scam clause of the December agreement.

Anutin told the UN General Assembly that Thailand regretted Cambodia's turn to UNCLOS conciliation after the two leaders had agreed in May to settle border issues bilaterally, and urged joint work on border security, demining and scam networks.

Prak Sokhonn told the UN General Assembly that the conflict had seriously eroded trust, that over 20,000 Cambodians still cannot return home, that Thailand should implement the December agreements and resume Joint Boundary Commission demarcation, and that the Charter sets no separate standard for powerful states.

text: On border incident management versus escalation prevention, the Declining / cautiously improving reading holds through 28 Sep: no exchange of fire, drone crossing or mine casualty has been reported since 12 Sep, and friction is confined to the Boundary Pillar 9 trench protested on 15 Sep and the Phnom Beng statue protested on 22 Sep. The capability signal remains the 22 Sep report of Rampage rockets and precision kits in the RTAF's FY2026 plan (single source), Thailand institutionalising stand-off strike rather than changing behaviour on the line. On ceasefire monitoring versus local force autonomy, the trigger has not fired, but the ASEAN observers' 16 Sep visit to the Rong Cham camp (13,259 people unable to return) and Sokhonn's 26 Sep figure of over 20,000 displaced show that consolidation of positions and barriers under the ceasefire, not fire, is the central grievance.

On regional mediation versus bilateral military signalling, the Background monitor status is contradicted: the contest sits at the UN podium, where Anutin on 24 Sep argued for bilateral mechanisms and Sokhonn on 26 Sep answered with the JBC and 'sovereign equality', while Khmer Times reports a Thai right of reply no Thai source had published by 28 Sep (single source). Neither side has convened the GBC or JBC this year, so the mechanisms both cite stay idle and ASEAN's observers are the only working channel; adaptability stays Low.

Al Jazeera and AFP reported that Machado's aide Claudia Macero said 'Maria Corina is trying every day to come home' after her own return and that the government has not commented (Al Jazeera; AFP via FMT).

27 Sep: Claudia Macero, 34, Vente Venezuela's communications chief, returned from the United States to Maiquetía airport, where hundreds of supporters sang the anthem, saying 'it is time to come home, it is time to recover the country'; she had left in May 2025 after more than a year sheltering in the Argentine embassy (AFP via FMT; Al Jazeera; Rio Times). Vente Zulia organiser Fernando Torrealba, detained by the National Guard during the Maracaibo caravan, was released the same afternoon without charges (El Nacional; El Pitazo; La Patilla). Comando con Venezuela's caravans drew hundreds in about eleven states including Caracas, Valencia, Maracaibo and Mérida to demand Machado's safe return, an electoral calendar and a 2027 presidential vote, and Machado said from Panama 'I will return very soon' (Infobae; El Diario; AP via ABC News; Al Jazeera). OilPrice's Tsvetana Paraskova put the cost of restoring output to historic levels at more than $100bn over a decade, noting NABEP's $100bn is a long-term requirement not committed capital, that only two rigs were active in August and that Chevron has pledged over $7bn (OilPrice).

27 Sep: Human-rights group Justicia, Encuentro y Perdón said 39 political prisoners were freed between 25 and 26 Sep from several prisons, among them eight women accused of 'narco-terrorism' in 2021, six people accused of working with the US in the 2020 'Operation Gideon' attempt and student Wilder Vásquez; Foro Penal confirmed 20; the releases followed the Friday negotiating session held with US approval and the government made no statement, with Foro Penal listing 344 political prisoners on 18 Sep (Al Jazeera/AFP; AP via ABC News; Rio Times).

26 Sep: The second round of US-backed government–opposition talks closed with Jorge Rodríguez and Dinorah Figuera naming a panel to vet Supreme Court nominees, widening access to blocked news websites and agreeing to reconvene in mid-October (Latin Times, single source). Lavrov told the UNGA Russia 'insists on and demands the prompt release' of Maduro and Cilia Flores and condemned the January operation as an invasion (TASS; Orinoco Tribune). Rodríguez marked the Strategic Operational Command anniversary stressing 'cohesion between the national executive and the military institution' (teleSUR); Reuters reported she returned from New York with 'no concrete agreements' and no election date and that the IDB's $2.5bn bridge loan still faces board opposition (Reuters via US News); Trump said 'I spoke about elections' with her (Reuters via Internazionale); Jorge Rodríguez denied blocking Machado's return and promised four elections 'within the constitutional timeframe' (El Nacional); a Guardian investigation relayed by Portside argued the NABEP deal is 'likely doomed' on legal grounds (Portside, single source).

24–25 Sep: Rodríguez and Trinidad and Tobago PM Persad-Bissessar issued a joint statement on 'a new era in bilateral relations' (Barbados Today); hundreds marched to the CNE in Caracas demanding Machado's return, new electoral authorities and a 2027 election (EFE via Infobae); Foreign Policy summarised Rodríguez's UN debut as a legitimacy win with Washington working with her on oil while declining to press for elections (Foreign Policy).

22–23 Sep: Trump held a pull-aside with Rodríguez at a UNGA reception on 22 Sep, their first encounter since Maduro's capture, covering debt restructuring, and Machado's team said three attempts to leave Panama had failed within 24 hours, her seventh blocked return (Reuters via US News); Rodríguez told the UNGA on 23 Sep 'there will be elections' in an 'orderly, institutional and verifiable' transition without a date (UN News); Reuters reported on 22 Sep that IDB president Goldfajn is working on a $2.5bn loan facing board pushback (Reuters via Investing.com).

history.note: Baseline: post-January 2026 operation; transition under US pressure.

timeline.text: US forces captured President Nicolás Maduro and his wife in overnight strikes across Caracas and three other states, flying them to New York to face narco-terrorism charges.
US-backed talks between Delcy Rodríguez's interim government and an opposition delegation led by Dinorah Figuera opened in Caracas, with Jorge Rodríguez heading the government side.
The White House announced 100-year concessions on 17 Venezuelan oil fields to North American Blue Energy Partners, with the US government taking a 35 percent stake.
Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere struck a go-fast vessel on Caribbean narco-trafficking routes, killing four, in the 70th US counter-cartel maritime strike.

Trump held a pull-aside meeting with interim President Delcy Rodríguez at a UN General Assembly reception, their first encounter since Maduro's capture, covering debt restructuring; the same day Machado's team said three attempts to leave Panama for Venezuela had failed within 24 hours, her seventh blocked return.

Addressing the UN General Assembly, Rodríguez pledged elections and a transition to 'full democracy' and said dialogue with the opposition had opened, but gave no date; Chile's Kast met her the same week to begin restoring consular ties.

The second round of US-backed government–opposition talks closed with a Supreme Court vetting panel and a mid-October third round, Rodríguez returned from New York with no concrete deals and no election date, Lavrov demanded Maduro's release at the UN, and Machado's movement called a nationwide caravan after Bonaire, Aruba and Curaçao refused her flight landing rights.

Rights groups reported 39 political prisoners freed on 25–26 September after the negotiating session, opposition caravans in about eleven states demanded Machado's return and a 2027 election, the National Guard briefly detained a Vente Venezuela organiser in Maracaibo, and Machado's communications chief Claudia Macero returned from exile to a crowd of hundreds at Maiquetía airport.

text: On counter-criminal operations versus sovereignty and escalation, the trigger has not fired: no strike has been reported since the 70th on 19 Sep, and Rodríguez's 26 Sep message to the Strategic Operational Command stressed executive–military 'cohesion' without mentioning the United States, while Lavrov's 26 Sep UNGA demand for Maduro's release is rhetorical. On border and maritime control versus illicit networks, the Established status is borne out from a new direction: the 28 Sep New York Times finding, relayed by Anadolu, that gold shipped under the Trump-authorised Minerven–Trafigura deal sits unsold because refiners cannot certify it free of Tren de Guayana protection money shows the illicit-mining economy reaching into the licensed trade Washington uses to reward Caracas, alongside a nine-day maritime pause and two Pacific refuelling interdictions in September.

On information operations versus political legitimacy, the Rising status is borne out and the bargaining sequence is producing tests: 39 prisoners freed on 25–26 Sep after a round that also named a Supreme Court vetting panel and a mid-October follow-up (single source), Claudia Macero's 27 Sep return to a crowd at Maiquetía as the first senior Vente figure back, caravans of hundreds in about eleven states, and a Vente Zulia organiser detained and released within hours. Returns and releases without a calendar suggest the government is testing how much opposition presence it can absorb while Machado stays in Panama; adaptability stays Medium.

changes: 28 Sep: AFP spokesman for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Roy Trinidad said the military 'categorically rejects the recent inflammatory statements' of Chinese diplomats and stands 'solidly behind' Teodoro, naming 'the continued illegal presence, coercive and aggressive conduct and the deceptive messaging of the Chinese Communist Party' as the source of tension, after the Chinese embassy in Manila called the defence secretary 'extremely anti-China' and accused him of 'smearing' China 'to gain political capital and serve his personal gains' over his weekend forum remarks on the 24 Sep blocking, the Alice Guo case and substandard Chinese-run steel plants; Teodoro separately said the West Philippine Sea would be an issue in the 2028 elections and told pro-China officials to resign; outlets date the embassy statement to 26, 28 or 29 Sep - stated as conflicting (PNA; GMA; Daily Tribune; Philstar).

27 Sep: the PLA Southern Theater Command and the China Coast Guard held a joint naval-air exercise around Scarborough Shoal 'in response to the acts made by certain countries' with the frigate Yulin, corvette Tianmen, replenishment ship Qinghaihu, a KJ-500 and the WZ-7 alongside cutters Wanshan, Chuanshan and Sifang; the same day US Ambassador Lipton 'strongly' condemned the 24 Sep blocking of the Second Thomas Shoal resupply and China's embassy told Washington to 'stop fanning the flames' (Reuters via GMA; Global Times; CGTN; Philstar; Daily Tribune).

22-25 Sep: the AFP counted 35 Chinese naval and coast guard ships at four features for 15-21 Sep, down from 48; China's defence ministry blamed the Philippine vessel for the 18 Sep collision near Xianbin Jiao; a PLAN warship shadowed the eleven-ship ADMM-Plus formation about 45 nm from Scarborough on 23 Sep and the eight-nation activity closed on 25 Sep (Palawan News; Xinhua; Philstar; ANI, single source on the closing date).

timeline.text: Chinese coast guard crew in an inflatable struck a Filipino sailor on the head with a baton near BRP Sierra Madre at Second Thomas Shoal, injuring him.

A PLAN warship shadowed the eleven-ship, eight-nation ADMM-Plus formation drilling off Zambales about 45 nautical miles from Scarborough Shoal, ignoring BRP Jose Rizal's radio invitation to join, as Beijing condemned Taiwan's transfer of a retired coast guard cutter to the Philippines.

Three PLAN warships, including two Type 022 missile boats, and five China Coast Guard cutters intercepted the MV Lapu-Lapu resupply run about 60 nautical miles from Second Thomas Shoal, a warship radioed that it would take 'compulsory measures' and the mission was suspended, the first blocked run since the July 2024 understanding.

Defence Secretary Teodoro said the Ayungin resupply mission 'will go on' and 'will not be deterred' after Beijing's coast guard accused Manila of breaking its commitments, while Malaysia's defence minister said Sabah's defences would be reinforced against a major-power clash spilling over.

The PLA Southern Theater Command and the China Coast Guard drilled boarding, forced towing and expulsion around Scarborough Shoal with a frigate, corvette, replenishment ship, KJ-500 and the WZ-7 drone 'in response to the acts made by certain countries', while the US ambassador in Manila condemned the 24 September blocking and China's embassy told Washington to 'stop fanning the flames'.

text: On grey-zone maritime coercion versus presence and resilience, the Established · Contested reading holds, now with a rhetorical layer: three days after the 24 Sep interception of the Lapu-Lapu run, the 27 Sep PLA-coast guard drill at Scarborough rehearsed boarding, forced towing and what Global Times called 'three-dimensional blockade', and on 28 Sep the Chinese embassy in Manila and the AFP traded attacks over Teodoro, the embassy calling him 'extremely anti-China' and the AFP naming 'deceptive messaging' as a source of tension. Presence at Sierra Madre still rests on a run Manila has vowed but not scheduled. On maritime domain awareness versus ambiguous attribution, the Rising status is borne out mainly on the Chinese side: SCMP reported on 28 Sep the WZ-7 high-altitude drone's first South China Sea deployment (single source), while Philippine agencies' counts of the 24 Sep interception still differ and the AFP's weekly count for the obstruction week has not appeared.

On distributed maritime posture versus force protection, the Rising · Contested rating is unchanged: the eight-nation ADMM-Plus sail ended on 25 Sep unmolested while a lightly escorted civilian boat was stopped, and Malaysia's 26-27 Sep Sabah defence drive shows a neighbour hedging rather than joining. Dispersed presence protects warships, not the supply line; adaptability is High for Manila's documentation and alliance messaging but untested at the point of resupply.

changes: 28 Sep: US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News Sunday that Trump 'continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world' and 'actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some, at one point', denied that the US$14 billion Taiwan package was delayed to appease Xi, said Trump is 'as strong on Taiwan as I've ever seen anybody' and that package discussions 'remain ongoing'; the State Department said 'US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China'; Trump then told reporters 'To China? You mean to Taiwan? ... I never heard of that one', 'maybe it's a good idea, but we didn't discuss it' and that Perdue 'was probably talking about Taiwan'; Guo Jiakun would not confirm the account, saying China builds its defence 'based on its needs'; Taiwan's representative in Washington Yu Da-wei told CBS he hoped the package 'can arrive as soon as possible' (Fortune; PBS; CNA; AP via Boston Globe; UDN, single source on Yu).

28 Sep: China's foreign ministry released a four-minute bilingual video, 'The Way Home', grounding Taiwan's status in the 1943 Cairo Declaration, the 1945 Potsdam Proclamation and UN Resolution 2758 and declaring that 'any force obstructing China's reunification is doomed to fail'; Reuters reported the same day that MAC deputy minister Shen Yu-chung said Xi is 'continuously trying to guide the World War Two historical narrative to be led by the People's Republic of China' and that Taipei will keep telling Washington the Republic of China was 'America's steadfast ally'; Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi said 'the US very much understands our defense needs' and policy is unchanged; the defence ministry logged 3 PLA sorties, 5 PLAN ships, 4 official ships and one median-line crossing for 27-28 Sep, taking September to 220 aircraft and 289 ships (Global Times; Reuters via US News; Taipei Times; ROC MND; Taiwan News).

27 Sep: at the groundbreaking of a drone development centre in Chiayi, President Lai said Taiwan 'must deepen cooperation with democratic partners and jointly build a safer and more resilient unmanned aircraft supply chain', citing Ukraine; the Cabinet's NT$145.7 billion (US$4.59 billion) supplementary defence request covers more than 600 coastal surveillance drones, over 40,000 coastal attack drones and a first batch of more than 100 small drone boats (Reuters via Baird Maritime; US News).

27-28 Sep: a Taiwanese national security official said Beijing 'failed to gain traction' in pressing Washington to cut arms sales and might 'turn to propaganda' using red-carpet images (single source); MAC deputy minister Shen said Xi's bid to fold Taiwan into US-China 'constructive strategic stability' and to trade Iran for Taiwan 'did not go smoothly'; KMT legislator Lee Yen-hsiu said the 'anti-China card' was 'ineffective' under a 'G2' framework and Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung rejected 'US-China joint management of Taiwan'; Deputy Foreign Minister Wu said China is 'aggressively pursuing narrative diplomacy' which the ministry will counter and Senator Ricketts backed the package on Fox (single source) (Taipei Times; UDN; Fox News).

26 Sep: Trump said he and Xi 'didn't talk about it too much ... He understands very much how I feel', Perdue said 'we're not changing the language', the White House fact sheet omitted Taiwan and Trump announced further meetings in November (China) and December (G20 Miami); People's Daily called Taiwan 'the first red line'; the MAC rejected the fact sheet's 'allies in World War II' line; Taiwan's coast guard seized a Chinese trawler and six crew inside restricted waters off Penghu (Bloomberg via Union-Bulletin; Taipei Times; UDN; NOWnews; Newtalk).

24-25 Sep: Beijing's readout quoted Xi asking the US to 'adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence'; four senators and seven House members wrote against withholding the package; Taiwan's foreign ministry rejected Xi's remarks as 'distorting facts'; a USCC-commissioned report named three Taiwan-US cables among the trans-Pacific systems most exposed to Chinese grey-zone action (PRC MFA; Reuters via ThePrint; Focus Taiwan; Taiwan News).

next.text: Whether the White House reconciles Perdue's 28 Sep account with Trump's denial in a formal statement on the summit's Taiwan exchange, any Trump-Lai contact, and whether US officials keep 'does not support' rather than 'oppose' independence; also whether Beijing's Taiwan Affairs Office or state media pick up the 'would he like to buy some' line as a bargaining-chip narrative.

timeline.text: After his Beijing summit with Xi, Trump declined to commit to a pending US$14 billion Taiwan arms package, saying he would decide shortly.

China Coast Guard began its first law-enforcement patrols east of Taiwan, radioing passing merchant ships for crew and destination details; a Putuoshan-led group repeated the patrol off Green Island in early September.
Taiwan began the ten-day live-fire phase of Han Kuang 42, mobilising reservists and fielding M1A2T tanks and the new Littoral Combat Command.
Taiwan's legislature approved a six-year NT$240 billion drone programme a week after the Cabinet approved a record NT$1.1225 trillion defence budget for 2027, equal to 3.01 percent of GDP.
Taiwan handed a decommissioned 500-tonne Kinmen-class coast guard cutter to the Philippine Coast Guard through an NGO, drawing a Taiwan Affairs Office rebuke two days later.

At the White House Xi urged the US to 'adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence'; Trump called it 'a very good meeting' and issued no readout, while four senators and seven representatives wrote against withholding the US$14 billion arms package.

Trump said he and Xi 'didn't spend a lot of time talking about Taiwan' and that Xi 'understands very much how I feel', Ambassador Perdue said 'we're not changing the language', Taipei's deputy foreign minister said arming Taiwan is an important US interest, and Taiwan's coast guard seized a Chinese trawler and six crew off Penghu.

findings.actor: US Ambassador to China David Perdue (Fox News Sunday) / State Department
findings.text: On 28 Sep 2026 Perdue said Trump 'continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world' and 'actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some, at one point', while denying the US$14 billion Taiwan package was delayed to appease Xi and calling Trump 'as strong on Taiwan as I've ever seen anybody'. The State Department replied that 'US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China', and a White House official said there are no plans to sell arms to China, leaving the summit's Taiwan exchange described by the envoy in terms Washington then had to walk back.

Asked about Perdue's account on 28 Sep 2026, Trump said 'To China? You mean to Taiwan? ... I never heard of that one', that 'maybe it's a good idea, but we didn't discuss it', that China would 'probably like to buy' superior US equipment, and that Perdue 'was probably talking about Taiwan'. In Beijing Guo Jiakun declined to confirm the exchange, saying China 'has always strengthened its national defense capabilities based on its needs', so Beijing neither owned nor denied a story that casts Taiwan's supply as negotiable.

findings.actor: PRC Ministry of Foreign Affairs (via Global Times)
findings.text: On 28 Sep 2026 the foreign ministry released a four-minute bilingual video titled 'The Way Home' that grounds Taiwan's status in the 1943 Cairo Declaration, the 1945 Potsdam Proclamation and UN Resolution 2758, opens with a patriotic song, casts Taiwan as a 'pearl' lost to Japanese invasion and restored at the surrender, and declares that 'any force obstructing China's reunification is doomed to fail' and 'that day will come'. Global Times framed reunification as 'an unstoppable historical trend', turning the summit's WWII framing into a produced legal-historical product for foreign audiences.

findings.actor: Taiwan Mainland Affairs Council (Shen Yu-chung) and Representative to the US Yu Da-wei
findings.text: Reuters reported on 27-28 Sep 2026 that Shen Yu-chung said Xi is 'continuously trying to guide the World War Two historical narrative to be led by the People's Republic of China' and that Taipei will keep conveying to Washington that 'the Republic of China was America's steadfast ally'. Taiwan's representative in Washington Yu Da-wei used archival photographs on CBS to correct the summit's history and said he hoped the US$14 billion package 'can arrive as soon as possible' (single source on the CBS appearance).

findings.actor: PLA (per ROC Ministry of National Defense)
findings.text: In the 24 hours to 06:00 on 28 Sep 2026 Taiwan's MND reported 3 PLA aircraft sorties, one of which crossed the median line into the northern ADIZ, 5 PLAN ships and 4 official ships, after 2 sorties and 11 ships the day before; September stood at 220 aircraft and 289 ship sightings. Air pressure has stayed at or below five sorties a day since the summit, leaving Beijing's message in the diplomatic and video channels rather than the strait.

A 28 Sep 2026 Modern Diplomacy essay, 'The Chip on the Table', argued that the terms of the US commitment to Taiwan are increasingly set in leader-level bargaining with Beijing 'not by repeal but by postponement', so that an arms sale is no longer routine implementation of US law but 'a disturbance of an agreed equilibrium, something to be justified, weighed and perhaps deferred'. It is one outlet's reading, published the day Perdue's disclosure gave the 'bargaining chip' frame new material (single source).

findings.actor: Taiwan national security official (via Taipei Times)
findings.text: On 28 Sep 2026 a Taiwanese national security official briefed that Beijing 'failed to gain traction' in pressing Washington to reduce arms sales and secured no tariff or high-tech relief, and that China had hoped to frame US-China ties as a stable relationship 'between equal powers' to deflect from economic problems. The official predicted that, lacking substantive wins, Beijing 'might turn to propaganda, using images of Xi receiving the red-carpet welcome to promote narratives that China is rising', and urged Taiwan to strengthen its 'silicon shield' and asymmetric defence (single source).

findings.actor: Taiwan Mainland Affairs Council (deputy minister Shen Yu-chung)
findings.text: On 27-28 Sep 2026 the MAC's Shen Yu-chung said Beijing had tried to place Taiwan inside US-China 'constructive strategic stability' but that Xi's push for a breakthrough on the strait 'did not go smoothly', and that Xi may have sought to trade cooperation on Iran for concessions on Taiwan, which Trump did not accept. He cited Ambassador Perdue's statement that Taiwan and Iran 'should be handled separately' as carrying 'subtext', turning the US envoy's words into Taipei's rebuttal of Beijing's linkage narrative.

findings.actor: KMT (legislator Lee Yen-hsiu) and DPP government (Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung)
findings.text: On 28 Sep 2026 KMT legislator Lee Yen-hsiu said the summit had made the 'anti-China card' that Washington and Taipei could jointly play 'ineffective', describing a 'G2' framework in which Trump deals transactionally under 'America First', and urged the DPP to seek concrete gains on chip tariffs, arms-sale approvals and diplomatic space instead. Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung replied that Taiwan and the US should manage China together rather than accept 'US-China joint management of Taiwan', keeping the opposition's 'G2' reading and the government's 'true partner' line in contest before the November elections.

On 27 Sep 2026 Wu said 'it would be in the US' vital interests to move the arms sales forward', that supporting Taiwan's democracy and self-defence aligns with 'mainstream countries', and that 'China has been aggressively pursuing narrative diplomacy' which the ministry will counter, citing the 21 Sep US-Japan-ROK and 22 Sep eight-nation statements on the strait. The ministry thus named Beijing's post-summit framing as a narrative campaign and set allied statements against it.

On 26 Sep 2026 Trump told reporters before leaving the White House that he and Xi 'didn't talk about it too much. Right now, it's fine. It's just moving along', adding 'he understands very much how I feel'. He neither restated the US 'does not support' formula nor accepted Xi's 'oppose independence' wording, leaving Beijing's readout as the fuller public account of the exchange.

On 26 Sep 2026 People's Daily's 'Zhong Sheng' commentary called Taiwan 'the core of China's core interests' and 'the first red line that cannot be crossed' in China-US relations, urged Washington to 'maintain the correct stance of opposing Taiwan independence', and cast 'constructive strategic stability' as a vision both leaders should 'transform into concrete action'. It kept Xi's summit wording in circulation after the White House fact sheet omitted Taiwan.

assessment.text: Evidence for 27 to 29 Sep 2026 shows both capitals messaging around Taiwan, Washington now the noisier. Beijing moved from readouts to a produced product: on 28 Sep the foreign ministry released a bilingual video, 'The Way Home', grounding Taiwan's status in Cairo, Potsdam and Resolution 2758 and calling any obstruction to reunification 'doomed to fail', while Guo Jiakun would not confirm Perdue's account and the PLA held to three sorties; no Taiwan Affairs Office line, fact-check or NSB count for the window was found. Washington's signal split on 28 Sep: Perdue told Fox that Trump had asked Xi whether he would 'like to buy some' US weapons, the State Department said US law prohibits it, and Trump said Perdue 'was probably talking about Taiwan', handing Beijing a bargaining-chip narrative for free. Taipei stayed on history and supply: the MAC said on 27-28 Sep it will keep telling Washington the Republic of China was America's wartime ally, Yu Da-wei used archival photos on CBS (single source), and Deputy Foreign Minister Chen said the US 'very much understands' Taiwan's needs.

items.whyNow: On 27 Sep Pakistan's newly inducted Hangor-class submarine fired an anti-ship cruise missile at a designated long-range target in the North Arabian Sea in its maiden live weapon firing, watched by the naval chief, a day after Rajnath Singh's 'every kind of strike' line and Modi's Mann Ki Baat message set India's declared threshold ahead of the 28 Sep tenth anniversary of the surgical strikes; the anniversary itself passed without a Line of Control incident, a Pakistani Foreign Office reply or an Indian Navy response, while ISPR kept labelling militants killed in Balochistan and Dera Ismail Khan 'India-backed' and Pakistan's water regulator forecast a 25% Rabi shortfall without naming India.
changes: 28 Sep: The tenth anniversary of the 2016 surgical strikes passed with commemorative coverage but no new Indian Army or Pakistani Foreign Office statement and no Line of Control incident reported; Interior Minister Naqvi said forces 'foiled the nefarious designs of Indian-sponsored terrorists' after four 'Fitna al-Khawarij' militants were killed in Dera Ismail Khan and two BLA men in Nokcha, Balochistan; IRSA warned of a 25% Rabi water shortage with reservoir carryover below 9.5 MAF, the lowest since 2021, without mentioning India; Defence Security Asia carried retired Vice Adm Sanjay Mahindru's warning that eight Hangor boats would be a 'massive headache' for the Indian Navy, and BusinessToday noted no official Indian response to the Hangor firing (The Express Tribune; Dawn; Defence Security Asia; BusinessToday).

27 Sep: ISPR said the newly inducted PNS/M Hangor 'accurately engaged a designated long-range target with an anti-ship cruise missile' in its maiden live weapon firing in the North Arabian Sea, witnessed by Chief of the Naval Staff Adm Naveed Ashraf as 'a major demonstration of operational readiness'; the missile, its range, the target and whether the boat fired submerged were not disclosed; Hangor is the first of eight Chinese-built AIP submarines (Dawn; The Express Tribune; BusinessToday).

27 Sep: Rajnath Singh told the NDTV Defence Conclave that 'as long as our neighbour continues the state policy of terrorism, India is completely ready for every kind of strike against terrorism', that 'there is a difference between peace and cowardice' and that India 'will not compromise on its security under any circumstances'; in Mann Ki Baat Modi said the 2016 surgical strikes 'demonstrated a new example of India's counter-terrorism policy' and that 'from the Balakot airstrike to Operation Sindoor' terror will draw 'a befitting response' (ANI/Daily Excelsior; The Tribune; Kashmir Observer).

27 Sep: ISPR said 'more than 71 terrorists' of 'Fitna al-Khawarij' and 'Fitna al-Hindustan' were killed in 96 hours of Operation Shaban and related actions in Quetta's Shaban area, Ziarat, Nushki and Mand, calling them 'backed and sponsored' by Afghanistan and India; Kabul and New Delhi did not respond and the toll is unverified (Geo News; TRT World; The News).

27 Sep: The IAF opened the operational phase of Tarang Shakti at Jodhpur (to 12 Oct) with Australia, the US, the UAE, France, Germany, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh flying F-35s, Rafales, F-16s, A400M, MRTT, KC-30A and C-130s near the Pakistan border, the F-35's first exercise on Indian soil; the F-35 count still conflicts between two-three and six (DD News; ANI/The Tribune; UNI).

25–26 Sep: Sharif told the UNGA that any attempt to 'stop, impede or divert' Pakistan's Indus share 'will be treated as an act of war'; Jaishankar replied that 'a serial practitioner of terrorism misrepresented facts' and that India's 'right to defend ourselves against terrorism will be exercised', India's right of reply warned 'terror will have consequences' and Pakistan's counter-reply accused India of 'weaponising water'; the same day Pakistan Navy ships Hunain and Yarmook seized 2,800 kg of narcotics in the Arabian Sea, PNS Hunain being the vessel that collided with INS Kolkata on 15 Sep (Dawn; The Tribune; The Express Tribune).

ignore.note: The window's movement is capability signalling and anniversary rhetoric: Hangor's maiden missile firing (27 Sep) with the missile and launch conditions undisclosed, Rajnath Singh's 'every kind of strike' and Modi's Mann Ki Baat lines, and ISPR's habit of labelling Baloch and TTP militants 'India-backed' (the 71-plus toll is unverified). No cross-border firing, no militant attack in J&K, no naval incident, no Pakistani Foreign Office reply and no Indian Navy response were reported through 28 Sep; the K2 drone delivery remains single-source. Retained because the declared threshold for a strike is public and low, the Indus and naval-collision disputes are unresolved, and Pakistan enters Rabi with a 25% water shortfall that could be politically attributed to India.

timeline.text: A Hague Court of Arbitration unanimously rules the Indus Waters Treaty remains fully in force and bars India from raising the Ratle dam; India rejects the award within hours as 'illegally constituted'.
Pakistani troops fire small arms and mortars across the Line of Control in Poonch's Mankote sector, a day after firing in Krishna Ghati; the Indian Army retaliates.

Indian destroyer INS Kolkata and Pakistani patrol vessel PNS Hunain collide in the North Arabian Sea during Pakistan's SEASPARK-26 exercise, the first physical military incident since May 2025; each side summons the other's charge d'affaires the next day and India later rejects Pakistan's account as 'the usual prevarication'.

India's envoy at the UN Human Rights Council tells Pakistan that 'neither terror nor theatrics' will repay its loans, New Delhi restates that the Indus arbitration court is illegally constituted, and Dar tells the OIC Contact Group that the treaty is binding under the August award.

Sharif tells the UN General Assembly that any attempt to stop, impede or divert Pakistan's share of the Indus waters 'will be treated as an act of war', calls Kashmir Pakistan's 'jugular vein' and credits Trump's intervention in the May 2025 conflict, while an Indian diplomat shakes his head in the hall.

Jaishankar tells the General Assembly that 'a serial practitioner of terrorism misrepresented facts' and that India's right to defend itself 'will be exercised', India's right of reply warns that 'terror will have consequences', and Pakistan's counter-reply accuses India of 'weaponising water' and exporting terrorism, as Exercise Tarang Shakti opens at Jodhpur with US F-35s.

Rajnath Singh says India is 'completely ready for every kind of strike against terrorism' while Pakistan pursues 'the state policy of terrorism' and Modi recalls the 2016 surgical strikes as the start of a policy running through Balakot and Operation Sindoor, as ISPR claims 71-plus 'India-backed' militants killed in Balochistan.

Pakistan's newly inducted Hangor-class submarine PNS/M Hangor fires an anti-ship cruise missile at a designated long-range target in the North Arabian Sea in its maiden live weapon firing, watched by naval chief Adm Naveed Ashraf, with the missile type and launch conditions undisclosed.

text: On cross-border strike and counterstrike versus escalation management, the Established · Contested status held through the 28 Sep surgical-strike anniversary without a kinetic test: no Line of Control firing has been reported since the 11 Sep Mankote incident (single source), the 15 Sep Arabian Sea collision has not recurred, and no Pakistani Foreign Office reply to Rajnath Singh's 27 Sep 'every kind of strike' line had appeared by 28 Sep. The declared threshold is now public and low, so the next mass-casualty attack in Jammu and Kashmir would carry a pre-announced response. On counterterrorism versus interstate deterrence, the Established rating is reinforced from both sides: Jaishankar's 26 Sep 'right to defend ourselves will be exercised' sits against ISPR's 27 Sep claim of 71-plus 'India-backed' militants killed in Balochistan (unverified) and Naqvi's 28 Sep 'Indian-sponsored' framing of four militants killed in Dera Ismail Khan, folding Pakistan's western insurgencies into the bilateral contest.

On air, missile and information operations versus nuclear-threshold ambiguity, the Contested edge moved to the sea: on 27 Sep PNS/M Hangor fired an anti-ship cruise missile at a long-range target in its maiden live firing, with the missile, range and launch depth undisclosed, while Tarang Shakti put US F-35s near the border and the Baykar K2 delivery report (single source) stands unconfirmed. Adaptability stays High; the window shows capability demonstration and messaging, not new employment.

items.whyNow: Stays Active: on 28 Sep a junta fighter jet dropped two bombs on the main wholesale market and adjacent bridge in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, at about noon, killing at least 33 and wounding 36 by the Arakan Army's and a senior rescue official's count, the deadliest strike in Rakhine since the December 2025 hospital bombing, far from any front and with no military comment; the same day Myanmar Now reported eight civilians including displaced people killed by 24–25 Sep strikes in Kawlin District near the Sagaing–Kachin border (single source) and floods in resistance-held Dawei District killed at least 13, while conscription arrests continued in Mon State and Yangon, the Sittwe–Ponnagyun and Chin fronts stayed under air cover and Malaysia's 29 Sep repatriation flight had not been reported as departed at review time.
changes: 28 Sep: A junta fighter jet dropped two bombs on Kyauktaw's main wholesale market and adjacent bridge at about noon, killing at least 33 vendors, shoppers and pedestrians and wounding 36 by the count of the Arakan Army and senior rescue official Wai Hun Aung, who said the site 'is quite far from the fighting and has nothing to do with the conflict'; the AA said the toll 'may continue to increase', a witness saw more than 30 bodies among smouldering wreckage, and the military did not comment (AP via Al Jazeera; Reuters via The Star and FMT; India Today). It is the deadliest strike in Rakhine since the December 2025 hospital bombing that killed at least 30.

28 Sep: Myanmar Now reported that air strikes on 24–25 Sep in Kawlin District near the Sagaing–Kachin border killed eight civilians including displaced people (Kawlin District PDF Battalion 1; single source); The Irrawaddy reported at least 13 dead and 30 missing in floods and landslides in resistance-held Dawei, Launglon and Thayetchaung townships, the heaviest local rainfall in 80 years, with more than 60 villages and 10,000 people affected (resistance figures; AFP put the feared toll at 10) (Myanmar Now; The Irrawaddy; The Star/AFP).

28 Sep: Mizzima's daily notes recorded continued detentions of young people for military service in Mon State townships and Yangon (HURFOM) and the NLD's 27 Sep 38th-anniversary statement recommitting to a federal democratic union; Malaysia's first repatriation of 1,476 Myanmar nationals on two Myanmar Navy warships and a hospital ship remained scheduled for 29 Sep with no departure reported at review time (Mizzima; Bernama).

27 Sep: DVB named Myanmar Air Force defector Nay Win Aung among at least six killed in the 24 Sep air strike on the NUG's 'Special Division Command' on the Bago–Mon corridor; the regime said the coordinates came from informants, which NUG spokesman Nay Phone Latt called psychological warfare; a Boom Myanmar fact-check rejected a claim that the Chinese-pressed MNDAA–junta talks in Naypyidaw (since 23–24 Sep) had collapsed; Bangladesh's Coast Guard seized 22 tonnes of Myanmar-origin scrap at Patenga (DVB; Myanmar Now; Boom Myanmar; BSS).

26 Sep: Ground fighting resumed on the Sittwe–Ponnagyun border after a roughly four-day pause that followed heavy junta losses in the 21 Sep push, with at least four aircraft including jets and Y-12s bombing Yae Yo Pyin, War Bo, Taw Kan and Pauktaw (Narinjara; single source); jets and Y-12s bombed Mindat, Kanpetlet, Saw and Htilin while the 1,000-troop DDI 25 column stayed put, and BNI reported the junta trucking casualties nightly from the Thabaung front to Pathein as the AA-led coalition closed on Artillery Battalion 344 at Yegyi (single source) (Narinjara; MoeMaKa/m.CDM; BNI).

25–26 Sep: Deputy Defence Minister Maj-Gen Aung Myo Thant told the Pyithu Hluttaw that artists, professionals, businesspeople and their children will be conscripted when their turn comes, as Mon State's 28th intake press-ganged 222 men and RFA's count reached 130,000-plus recruits since 2024; The Irrawaddy reported students being entered in Mandalay draft lotteries as Batch 28 quotas go unfilled (Mizzima; BNI/IMNA; RFA; The Irrawaddy).

history.note: FPV strike on Tada-U airbase, failed junta Rakhine offensive and AA counter-offensive, ASEAN seat decision pending.

timeline.text: Min Aung Hlaing is inaugurated as president of Myanmar's quasi-civilian military government in Naypyitaw, and on 21 April offers armed groups peace talks with a 100-day deadline that the KNU, CNF and NUG reject.
The military launches 'Operation 4926', a combined land, naval and air offensive against the Arakan Army across Sittwe, Ponnagyun, Kyaukphyu and Gwa townships in Rakhine State.
Six fibre-optic FPV drones strike Tada-U airbase near Mandalay; resistance says Yak-130 jets were hit, the junta says all were intercepted, and international flights are cancelled.
The Arakan Army's counter-offensive seizes four junta outposts on the Sittwe-Ponnagyun border, including positions near Minchaung Bridge and the Shwe Min Gan naval station.

A junta column of over 180 vehicles and about 1,000 troops with MLRS, drones and signal jammers reaches the DDI 25 weapons plant in Saw Township to renew the offensive on Mindat and Kanpetlet in southern Chin State.

Three junta jets bomb the National Unity Government's regional command near Kyaikto, killing at least six including Air Force defector Nay Win Aung, as the Arakan Army repels a two-week junta attempt on the Maei pass at Mindon, Malaysia sets 29 Sep to begin deporting Myanmar migrants, Myanmar recalls its ambassador to Thailand, a Delhi court lets the foreign drone trainers leave India and an MNDAA delegation opens Chinese-pressed talks in Naypyidaw.

Ground fighting resumes on the Sittwe–Ponnagyun border after a four-day pause forced by junta losses on 21 Sep, with jets and Y-12s bombing Yae Yo Pyin, War Bo and Pauktaw, while residents on the Rakhine–Ayeyarwady border report the junta trucking hundreds of casualties nightly from Thabaung to Pathein.

A junta fighter jet drops two bombs on the main wholesale market and adjacent bridge in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, at about noon, killing at least 33 people and wounding 36 by the Arakan Army's and a senior rescue official's count, the deadliest strike in Rakhine since the December 2025 hospital bombing, with no comment from the military.

text: On distributed resistance versus state airpower, the Established · Contested status is borne out in its harshest form: ground pushes stall and aircraft are turned on population centres. On 28 Sep a jet dropped two bombs on Kyauktaw's main market at midday, killing at least 33 and wounding 36 by the Arakan Army's and a rescue official's count, at a site 'quite far from the fighting'; on 26 Sep the Sittwe–Ponnagyun push restarted under jet and Y-12 cover after a four-day pause (single source), and strikes on 24–25 Sep in Kawlin District killed eight civilians (single source). Airpower is not converting into ground gains, and conscription now reaches Mandalay students and the children of professionals. On commercial UAS and improvised systems versus conventional advantage, the Rising status held on the regime side through the window: the informant-cued 24 Sep Kyaikto strike and the 26 Sep drone-bomb on a Kanbalu monastery show cheap targeting being institutionalised; no new resistance airbase strike was reported.

On fragmented governance versus logistics and civilian resilience, the Established status is reinforced by parallel stresses: floods in resistance-held Dawei killed at least 13 on 27–28 Sep in villages only resistance administrations reach, Beijing kept the MNDAA at the Naypyidaw table, and Malaysia's 29 Sep repatriation flight now lands a day after Kyauktaw. Adaptability stays High; escalation against civilians is the pattern, not a change of method.
